Review Body:
I have very little positive to say about this book. I like Melania and have talked to someone who knows her personally who says she is one of the kindest, most caring persons he knows. I wanted to love the book but I could barely get through it and skimmed a lot of it. I think the reading of it would make people like her less so if she meant to promote herself, this is a huge fail!

The writing is terrible. I realize she is not a writer and maybe there is a barrier in culture and nuance of language, but the constant "I did this, I did that, I'm compassionate, I'm loving......" was a bit eye rolling. She needed a good editor or a ghost writer.

It was very repetitive and read more like a journal in areas...not even chronological. At times I had to go back because I thought I had dozed off when a new paragraph in the same chapter started on a completely unrelated subject...very strange. Even some of the photos were odd choices.... I got the feeling she couldn't make a decision on photos so just threw them all in, even if unflattering.

The black matte cover jacket is awful and gets oil spots on it from just holding the book making it look horrible in minutes. I didn't have any problem with the binding like others have said in reviews but the book was indeed expensive and not worth the price. I feel as if she had some kind of publication deadline and didn't give enough time to do this job well or even that someone sabotaged her into thinking it was great!

In contrast I read Free, Melania : the Unauthorized Biography by Kate Bennet in late 2019. I would never have picked that book up but it was given to me by my son who didn't realize it was supposed to be negative. I gave that book 2 stars, so it also was not great but even though it was supposed to be a "hit job", Kate described Melania quite well. I remember thinking Melania must be a pretty good person because the only bad things Kate could come up with revolved around Melania's shopping habits. I also learned a lot about life in the White House as Kate Bennet was the only journalist in the White House press corps to cover solely Melania Trump.

After reading Melania, the only interesting item I've come away with is this.

She shared the tradition of the outgoing president allowing the incoming president to check out the White House and plan for their move and renovation of rooms etc (expecially with a 10 year old boy moving in). This time is usually over the Christmas holidays when the sitting president's family is out of the White House in some other location. She wrote that the Trump staff sent a request but did not receive a response for weeks making it very difficult to organize the visit with the people needed. That was part of the reason she finished off the school year with Baron in NYC.
She mentioned Baron was 10 and the children's rooms were feminine since there had not been a boy child in the White House since Kennedy. She wanted to make the transition as easy as possible for him. Incidentally, as I was reading this part, I then heard a brief news item that the Trumps were invited to the White House this Christmas Season.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on November 20, 2024
Review Body:
Melania by Melania Trump is a masterclass in vacuity, a memoir that promises insight into the life of one of the most enigmatic and scrutinized figures of modern politics but delivers little more than an exercise in self-promotion. The book is a glossy, surface-level account that skirts the most meaningful questions about her life, reducing the complex reality of her experiences to a series of clichés and vague, lifeless platitudes.

Rather than offering genuine introspection or revealing new perspectives, Melania's narrative is predictably distant and calculated, mirroring the aloofness that has defined her public persona. There is little substance in her reflections, only a repetitive parade of tired tropes about beauty, family, and a vague sense of American patriotism, all packaged in a way that feels more like a branding effort than an authentic memoir.

The writing itself is excruciatingly shallow. Melania, as a writer, displays a complete lack of depth, offering up sparse, almost mechanical descriptions of events and emotions. It’s clear that this book was written not for personal expression, but as a carefully curated product designed to sell a particular image—an image that remains deliberately impenetrable. Her reluctance to delve into any meaningful aspects of her personal life or thoughts on her controversial marriage to Donald Trump only adds to the sense that this book is nothing more than an exercise in vanity and image management.

In terms of narrative, the book meanders with no clear sense of direction, lacking both a cohesive structure and a compelling arc. Her experiences as First Lady are brushed over with little insight into the complexities of her role. There is no substantial reflection on the controversies surrounding her husband's presidency or her own public persona. Instead, readers are left with a sanitized, glorified version of Melania's life, where her true thoughts remain carefully guarded.

Melania by Melania Trump isn’t a memoir—it's a missed opportunity, a hollow text that fails to humanize its subject or offer any real connection. It’s a book that feels entirely detached from any real human experience, leaving behind only the stark reminder of how artfully crafted public images can be, and how little substance often lies beneath.

Review Body:
I read a copy from my library and was quite disappointed as found this book lacks depth and serves more as a vehicle for propaganda than a genuine exploration of Melania's life. The memoir covers her childhood, modeling career, and marriage to Donald Trump, but is vague and superficial, filled with generic cliches lacking in substantial insights about her personal experiences or political views.

While Melania touches on her upbringing in Slovenia and her experiences in the fashion industry, she glosses over significant historical contexts, such as the civil war in Yugoslavia and the oppressive atmosphere of communism. Similarly, Melania's portrayal of her relationship with Donald Trump is notably detached. The memoir lacks unique details or emotional depth, often depicting their interactions in a cold light. For instance, she describes a post-election moment between them that feels more like a business exchange than a personal connection.

While Melania does touch upon political issues, including her stance on abortion rights, these discussions often feel like calculated moves rather than genuine expressions of belief. Her commentary on significant events during her husband's presidency is sparse and lacks personal insight -- its obviously more of an attempt to reshape public perception rather than provide an honest account. She fails to grapple with the complexities of her marriage or her role as First Lady, and I was left with a sense of emptiness rather than clarity about Melania's life and values.
